narrative:
The model determined that you have a 70% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this predicted outcome, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this decision were your LSAT score, your academic performance in the third year of law school, and your family income level. Your LSAT score was the single biggest reason for the negative outcome. At 32, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, and this lower score strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure.

Your third-year class ranking worked in your favor. Placing in the 8th decile is noticeably stronger than the average 5.8 decile seen among accepted students, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. However, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the other factors.

Your middle family income bracket also contributed to the prediction of failure, though less strongly than your LSAT. Among accepted students, a much higher share come from upper-middle or high-income families, so your background placed you at a statistical disadvantage.

Given these results, the most productive next step is to focus on significantly improving your LSAT performance. Retaking the test and aiming for a score closer to or above 37 would likely shift future predictions in your favor and strengthen any re-application.
